{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-az-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"a0426fa17a1c210c9367ecf3efd279258eab2659cf4a7f34f93e629b41d8c450","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-az-class-d:lineage:73","source_registry_sha256":"6dbbc2d22fea619728bdb90038a4aedf3afc07eab652b3f97027c9c69aaadaf4","source_liveness_sha256":"1c5753487760cbe2044d84b5696121c7181af61815b598d89d5ce158abf5fe43"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Hydroplaning recovery, flooded washes and flood liability, fog, snow and ice, headlight use, night driving, highway hypnosis and wrong-way drivers","heading":"C — Recovering from a hydroplane, flash floods and flooded washes, the flood-barricade liability rule, fog, snow and ice braking, low-visibility and night headlight rules, highway hypnosis, and how to avoid and respond to a wrong-way driver","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Recovering from a hydroplane, flash floods and flooded washes, the flood-barricade liability rule, fog, snow and ice braking, low-visibility and night headlight rules, highway hypnosis, and how to avoid and respond to a wrong-way driver
Knowledge domain: what to do when your car hydroplanes, why flooded washes must never be crossed and who pays when a driver goes around flood barricades, how to drive in fog, snow and ice, when to use low and high beams, how to stay alert on long drives, and how to avoid, react to and report a wrong-way driver.

FACT_ID: sec17-F01 | anchor: A01
If your car hydroplanes, take your foot off the accelerator and do not brake. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F02 | anchor: A01
While hydroplaning, avoid steering changes if you can and hold the wheel firmly until the tires grip the road again. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F03 | anchor: A01
Heavy rain often causes flash floods in Arizona washes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F04 | anchor: A01
Never cross a flooded wash, because the water can stall your engine, hide potholes and carry your vehicle downstream. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F05 | anchor: A01
Judge how deep water is by looking at parked cars or other objects along the road and by watching what other vehicles do. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F06 | anchor: A01
Two vehicles should not meet in deep water, so one should drive all the way through before the other starts from the opposite side, which lowers the risk of stalling from waves. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F07 | anchor: A01
You may be charged for emergency response costs if you or your vehicle has to be removed from a flooded road. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F08 | anchor: A01
Drive through water at a slow and steady speed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F09 | anchor: A01
Pressing the brakes lightly with your left foot while driving through water may help keep them dry. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F10 | anchor: A01
After leaving water, test your brakes, because wet brakes may grab suddenly or pull to one side. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F11 | anchor: A01
Dry wet brakes by accelerating slowly while holding the brake pedal down gently. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F12 | anchor: A01
A driver who goes around flood barricades is liable for the cost of any emergency response needed to remove the driver or passengers when the vehicle becomes inoperable on a public street or highway. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F13 | anchor: A01
The expenses of an emergency response are the reasonable costs that responding agencies directly incur when they make an appropriate response. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F14 | anchor: A01
Fog reflects light and can bounce your own headlights back into your eyes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F15 | anchor: A01
In fog, use only your low beams and follow the road edge markings. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F16 | anchor: A01
Even light fog cuts visibility and your ability to judge distance, so slowing down is very important. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F17 | anchor: A01
Fog can thicken from one moment to the next, so keep adjusting your speed and be ready for emergency maneuvers. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F18 | anchor: A01
If fog gets too thick, pull off the road, turn off your headlights and wait there until the fog lifts. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F19 | anchor: A01
Snow limits visibility, so you need your headlights on both to see and to be seen. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F20 | anchor: A01
Snow often hides lane markings completely, and drivers may drift away from the road edge and pass closer to one another. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F21 | anchor: A01
Snow or ice between your tires and the road greatly reduces traction and, in the manual's words, adds at least 6 seconds to the distance you need to stop. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F22 | anchor: A01
On a slippery surface you keep the most traction and control while the front tires are rolling, so the car responds better to steering than to braking. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec17-F23 | anchor: A02
If you brake on ice or another slippery surface, start gently and build pressure as you feel the tires grip. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F24 | anchor: A02
On a slippery surface, never brake so hard that the wheels lock. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F25 | anchor: A02
If the wheels lock, ease slightly off the brakes without letting go completely, then brake and ease off again, repeating the cycle. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F26 | anchor: A02
In winter, drive with caution and avoid sudden changes in speed or direction. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F27 | anchor: A02
Before you start driving in winter, clear the snow and ice from every window and light. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F28 | anchor: A02
Snow tires or chains help prevent skids and shorten stopping distances. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F29 | anchor: A02
Packed snow behaves much like ice, so slow down before you stop or turn on it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F30 | anchor: A02
Watch for ice on bridges and in shady spots, because bridge surfaces freeze before the rest of the road. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F31 | anchor: A02
Turn on your low-beam headlights in sun glare, rain, dust or any other condition where other drivers may not see your vehicle clearly. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F32 | anchor: A02
On rural roads, your headlights help a driver who is thinking of passing in your lane see that you are coming. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F33 | anchor: A02
Reduced visibility, glare from oncoming headlights and objects you cannot see in the road combine to make night driving hazardous. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F34 | anchor: A02
As soon as daylight begins to fade in the late afternoon, turn on your headlights rather than your parking lights. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F35 | anchor: A02
Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise, but remember that other drivers may not have switched theirs on. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F36 | anchor: A02
Never drive so fast that you cannot stop within the distance your headlights let you see. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F37 | anchor: A02
Use low beams when driving on city or town streets. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F38 | anchor: A02
On highways, use high beams only when no oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F39 | anchor: A02
Switch to low beams whenever you meet oncoming traffic so you do not blind the other driver. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F40 | anchor: A02
When following another car, use low beams once you are within 200 feet of it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F41 | anchor: A02
If an oncoming driver does not dim the high beams, do not stare into them, but glance at the right side of the road and then ahead to track the other vehicle. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec17-F42 | anchor: A03
Keep up that glance to the right and ahead until you are past the oncoming vehicle with bright lights. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F43 | anchor: A03
Highway hypnosis, also called white line fever, is a trance-like state that can set in during long periods of highway driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F44 | anchor: A03
Whenever you feel tired on a trip, pull over and rest. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F45 | anchor: A03
The radio and fresh air can help you fight off highway hypnosis. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F46 | anchor: A03
On long trips, stop every hour to walk and exercise so you stay alert. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F47 | anchor: A03
Drive defensively at every hour, staying aware of conditions and surroundings so you can take evasive action against a hazard such as a wrong-way driver. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F48 | anchor: A03
Do not tailgate, so that if the car ahead swerves to avoid a wrong-way driver you have time to react as well. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F49 | anchor: A03
Wrong-way drivers are usually in the left or HOV lane, yet they get onto highways from the right by using off-ramps. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F50 | anchor: A03
Wrong-way drivers are often impaired, which makes their movements unpredictable. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F51 | anchor: A03
On a divided highway, if a vehicle is coming at you head-on, lift your foot off the gas to slow down. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F52 | anchor: A03
Make sure no vehicle is beside you, then steer away from the wrong-way driver. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F53 | anchor: A03
Once you reach a safe place, call 911 and report the wrong-way driver. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F54 | anchor: A03
When ADOT is alerted to a possible wrong-way driver, overhead message boards on that part of the freeway show a wrong-way driver alert. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F55 | anchor: A03
If you see a wrong-way driver alert on an overhead board, move safely toward the nearest exit as soon as you can. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F56 | anchor: A03
Never drive while distracted or impaired, and never let an impaired person drive. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec17-F57 | anchor: A03
Most wrong-way crashes are caused by impaired drivers. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

Misconceptions: braking hard during a hydroplane makes it worse, so you lift off the gas and do not brake; low beams, not high beams, work best in fog; a wrong-way driver is usually in the left or HOV lane even though they entered from the right; locked wheels are freed by easing off the brake slightly, not by releasing it completely.
Mnemonics: Lift, do not brake, when you hydroplane; never cross a flooded wash; low beams in fog, rain, dust and glare; ease off the gas and steer away from a wrong-way driver.
Glossary: wash means a dry creek bed that can flood suddenly after heavy rain; highway hypnosis means a trance-like state from long, monotonous highway driving; wrong-way driver means a driver traveling against traffic on a divided highway; inoperable means no longer able to be driven.
Dynamic facts: the flood-response liability rule is statutory and can be amended, and ADOT's overhead wrong-way alert system and the freeways it covers can change.
